uncited: Anti-Aliasing and Filtering in volume rendering addresses the visual artifacts caused by undersampling, including jagged edges, flickering, and high-frequency noise, by smoothing the transition between discrete samples and continuous geometry.

This family encompasses methods that operate at different stages of the pipeline: pre-filtering data to prevent discretization errors, spatial filtering during rasterization (such as splatting), and post-processing screen-space blurs.

It is distinct from sibling methods like [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques](2787-interpolation-and-sampling-techniques.md) because it focuses on the suppression of high-frequency components in the final image or intermediate buffers rather than the accuracy of individual sample retrieval.
**Image Representation**: The input is an image $L$, defined as a discrete two-dimensional function $L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$.
**Color Space and Range**: The color channels (red, green, blue) are assumed to be non-negative real numbers.
**Screen-Space Constraint**: Many techniques in this family operate exclusively on information currently visible on the screen.
**Convolution Basis**: Many techniques apply a filter to the original image or splat footprint, typically using neighborhood-based convolution.
The concept of filtering in volume rendering has evolved alongside hardware capabilities.
